newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks, baht seen diving on Amnuay quit news.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks, baht seen diving on Amnuay quit news.

text.p: Thailand's battered stock market and the baht are seen dropping sharply on the news that Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan will resign from his post on Thursday, brokers and analysts said.
"The stock and money markets will be greatly affected by the expected resignation of the finance minister," said Thanadech Mahapokai of Book Club Finance and Securities.
The stock market is languishing at a new 98-month low after closing 14.78 points lower at 482.94 on Wednesday on rumours that Amnuay planned to resign.
In the offshore market, the baht was quoted much lower at 24.900/000 in the morning compared with 23.530/630 late on Wednesday.
An Amnuay aide late on Wednesday confirmed that the minister planned to resign on Thursday and would submit his letter to Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh.

Political sources said the appointed Amnuay wanted to quit because of pressure from political rivals within Chavalit's six-party coalition unhappy with the minister's style and his handling of the sluggish Thai economy and associated problems.
An official in the prime minister's department said Amnuay, who is also concurrently deputy prime minister, would submit his letter of resignation depending on the convenience of the premier.
"Amnuay's resignation will discredit this government. The credibility of the government is already bad and so far Chavalit does not know who could succeed Amnuay," said Thanadech.
Other analysts said there might be a slim chance Amnuay may remain in his job because he appeared to be buying time to negotiate his position vis-a-vis his rivals with the premier.
"The fact that he has yet to hand in his resignation to the premier looks like he is buying time to negotiate and maybe get his political rivals off his back," said an analyst at a local brokerage.
"However, if his resignation is accepted by the premier then he will be the fall guy for this government and this will also lead to altering of the course of Thai economic policy," said the analyst.
Other analysts expected changes in the way the Thai baht is weighted against a basket of currencies dominated by the dollar as a possible change in sight after Amnuay's departure.
Some speculated a baht devaluation, which Amnuay has long resisted, may be likely in the near future as well.

The baht has been the target of foreign speculators who have been betting it will be devalued. The last attack on the currency was in mid-May and it forced the central bank to adopt currency controls to ward off foreign speculators.
"His resignation and entrance of a new personality could force Thailand to make some drastic changes in its economic policy," said an analyst.

Thailand's economic downturn, the worst in more than a decade, has led to troubles in the ailing finance and glutted property sectors, high interest rates affecting businesses, speculative attacks on the baht and slowing consumer spending.
